bibliographic.title: Considering the possibilities and pitfalls of Generative Pre-trained Transformer 3 (GPT-3) in healthcare delivery
bibliographic.authors: Diane M. Korngiebel; Sean D. Mooney
bibliographic.citation_apa: Korngiebel, D. M., & Mooney, S. D. (2021). Considering the possibilities and pitfalls of Generative Pre-trained Transformer 3 (GPT-3) in healthcare delivery. npj Digital Medicine, 4, 93. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-021-00464-x

methodology.technology_context: GPT-3; Natural Language Processing; eHealth; conversational text generation

eligibility.decision_rationale: Commentary article focused on opportunities and cautions for deploying GPT-3 and similar NLP applications in healthcare-related conversational contexts. Highly relevant to regulated-domain LLM risks and human oversight, but not an empirical or operational study of conversational governance mechanisms such as guardrails, audit, tracing, or compliance frameworks.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial full text was supplied (predominantly page 1); commentary classification and governance-relevance should be confirmed against the complete article.

appraisal.notes: Perspective commentary appropriately frames healthcare deployment risks for GPT-3 but provides no empirical sampling, data collection, or operational governance evaluation. Arguments are supported mainly by cited prior work and illustrative examples rather than original study data.

cerqual.explanation: The article coherently links GPT-3 conversational use in healthcare to harm, bias, and human-replacement limits, but as a brief commentary it offers limited depth on operational governance and no primary evidence base for implementation controls.

coding.theme: Risks and limits of conversational GPT-3 in regulated healthcare
coding.subtheme: Human oversight and harm prevention in eHealth NLP
rq_alignment: governança de IA generativa em contextos regulados
controle de risco e supervisão humana

synthesis.main_claim: GPT-3 and similar generative NLP applications may enter healthcare and eHealth contexts, but they should not replace human clinical conversations; their deployment requires careful assessment of harm, bias, feasibility, and stakeholder risk.
synthesis.contribution: Provides an early regulated-domain framing of GPT-3 conversational pitfalls, including suicide-support failure in mental health simulation, demographic and religious bias, extremism priming, and a risk-based prioritization lens for healthcare applications.
synthesis.limitations: Commentary format without original empirical evaluation; partial supplied text prevents verification of any additional recommendations beyond page 1; does not address operational governance tooling such as guardrails, logging, tracing, audit, or formal compliance mechanisms.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on healthcare conversational LLM risks, human oversight limits, and bias-related accountability concerns; not as central operational evidence on conversational governance implementation.

evidence.claim: Article is a commentary on GPT-3 possibilities and pitfalls in healthcare delivery
evidence.excerpt: COMMENT OPEN Considering the possibilities and pitfalls of Generative Pre- trained Transformer 3 (GPT-3) in healthcare delivery

evidence.claim: Published in peer-reviewed npj Digital Medicine in 2021
GPT-3 could be deployed in healthcare contexts historically based on human-to-human interaction
evidence.excerpt: they could be deployed in healthcare-related contexts that have historically comprised human-to-human interaction

evidence.claim: Generative conversational AI will not replace human clinical conversation in the foreseeable future
evidence.excerpt: AI that generates text and conversations, such as GPT-3, will not replace a conversation with another human being for the foreseeable future in clinical settings

evidence.claim: GPT-3 cannot interact with patients instead of healthcare providers or support personnel
evidence.excerpt: it cannot interact with patients in lieu of healthcare providers or healthcare support personnel

evidence.claim: Simulated mental health use case showed harmful conversational failure
evidence.excerpt: testing the use of GTP-3 for mental health support using a simulated patient; the model supported the patient’s suggestion of suicide

evidence.claim: GPT-3 cannot dynamically adjust conversation for tone or body language
evidence.excerpt: cannot dynamically adjust a conversation or interaction for tone or body language

evidence.claim: GPT-3 exhibits demographic and religious bias patterns
evidence.excerpt: GPT-3 showed associations between gender and certain jobs; often the default was male. Negative sentiments were associated with Black race and positive with Asian race. Islam was more often associated with terrorism-related words than were other religions

evidence.claim: GPT-3 can be primed for harmful extremist text generation
evidence.excerpt: GPT-3 is easy to prime for harmful text generation promoting extremism and terrorist activities, including Nazism and QAnon

evidence.claim: Healthcare NLP applications should assess risk, feasibility, and return on investment
evidence.excerpt: evaluation of AI health and healthcare applications that produce natural language should assess their risk, feasibility, and return on investment—including prioritizing improved patient care

evidence.claim: Lower-risk GPT-3 applications should be prioritized before higher-risk ones
evidence.excerpt: Realistic applications of GPT-3 must start in areas of high value, high feasibility, and low risk for all stakeholders, including (at a minimum) patients, clinicians, administrators, and payers

evidence.claim: No empirical sample or study design is described in the supplied text
evidence.excerpt: In this article, we brieﬂy introduce some opportunities and cautions that would accompany advanced Natural Language Processing applications deployed in eHealth
